title: Simple Algorithms for Bad Triangle Transversals with Applications to Correlation Clustering
claim: Greedily removing edges from an optimal solution can unintentionally create a new forbidden structure, so the fix is not locally safe.
layout: single panel, six labeled nodes in a 2x3 grid, dashed edges forming a rectangle
description: A single minimal black-and-white graph drawing with six vertices as filled dots, labeled with italic math letters. Top row has c, b and a. Bottom row has d, e and f. Four dashed lines join c, b, e and d into a tall rectangle: c–b, b–e, e–d and d–c. These are the negative edges. Vertices a and f stand isolated on the right with no drawn edges, because all other pairs are positive and left undrawn. The eye goes first to the dashed rectangle, which is a four-cycle containing exactly the negative edges. It shows a small counterexample in which removing edges leaves a bad cycle. There is no color, arrows or text beyond the vertex labels.
caption: Removing edges from an optimal \badt solution can lead to a bad cycle. Dashed edges are negative edges, all other pairs are connected by a positive edge (not drawn).
abstract: The Bad Triangle Transversal (BTT) problem asks for the smallest set of edges that need to be removed from a given signed graph, so that the resulting graph does not have a bad triangle. Here, a bad triangle is a triangle with exactly one negative edge. Several 2-approximations for BTT are proposed in this paper. On the hardness side, we show that BTT is NP-hard to approximate with factor better than $\frac{2137}{2136}$ on complete graphs. Our reduction also works for Correlation Clustering (CC), the Cluster Deletion problem (CD) and the Minimum Strong Triadic Closure problem (MinSTC). Lastly, we show that the BTT and CC optima are within a factor of 3/2 in complete graphs, by describing a pivot procedure that transforms transversals into clusters.
